::: {.lead}
In fourteen lectures you learned to keep your files in order, to use AI
tools with care, and to make documents in Word and sheets in Excel. In this
review you go through all of it once more, in four parts (@fig-map). Each
part gives the **main points**, one **example** from the Sunrise Company,
the most **common mistake**, and a short **lab task**. At the end, a
mini-game takes you through one busy day of Huda, the office manager.
:::

{{< glossary file-path cloud-storage synchronization backup prompt check-ai-output heading-style table-of-contents formula absolute-reference filter-data chart >}}

## 15.1 Files and the cloud (lectures 1, 2, 5, 6)

::: {.callout-important title="Main points 15.1 — Files"}
- Use **one account** (your university account) for Office, e-mail and the
  e-learning platform.
- Keep files in **folders**; a good name has the date first and says what
  it is: `2026-11-03_report.docx`.
- **Sync** copies every change to your other devices (also mistakes); a
  **backup** keeps an extra copy you can go back to.
- Share with a **link** only for the people who need it, with the right
  permission (can view or can edit).
:::

![A folder tree (lecture 2).](../week-01/images/folder-tree.png){width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.1 — Huda's files"}
1. Huda saves the price list as `2026-11-03_price-list.xlsx` in
   *Sunrise › Shop*.
2. The folder is in OneDrive: the file syncs to her phone.
3. She shares it with Rana only, "can edit". Nobody else can open it.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that sync is a backup. If you delete a file on the phone, sync
deletes it on the computer too.
:::

{{< sim file="../week-03/sims/share-settings.html" poster="../week-03/sims/share-settings.png" title="Share Settings: who and what?" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your study folder"}
1. In OneDrive (or Documents), make the folders *Digital Skills › Lab* and
   *Digital Skills › Online*.
2. Move three of your files from this course into the right folder, with
   good names.
3. Share one file with a classmate, "can view" only.

*Your result:* a screenshot of your folders.
:::

## 15.2 AI tools and prompts (lectures 3, 4, 9, 10)

::: {.callout-important title="Main points 15.2 — AI"}
- AI tools are good at **first drafts, summaries, rewriting and
  translation**; they can **make up facts** (hallucinations).
- A clear **prompt** has a **task**, the **context** (the facts) and the
  **format** (length, tone, form).
- Improve the answer with a **follow-up** prompt.
- **Check every answer** against your facts, and never type real personal
  data into an AI tool.
:::

![The parts of a prompt (lecture 4).](../week-02/images/prompt-parts.png){width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.2 — A notice for the staff"}
1. Prompt: "Write a notice to staff: the office closes on Thursday at 1 pm
   for cleaning. Friendly, 3 sentences."
2. The answer adds: "The shop also closes at 1 pm." That is wrong.
3. Huda corrects it: "The shop stays open until 6 pm."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Copying an AI answer straight into a letter or a report. Read it and check
every name, date and number first.
:::

{{< sim file="../week-02/sims/weak-spots.html" poster="../week-02/sims/weak-spots.png" title="Weak Spots: what is wrong with this AI answer?" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Prompt and check"}
1. Ask an AI tool for a 3-sentence notice: "The library closes at 2 pm on
   Sunday." Use task, context and format.
2. Check the answer. Did it add or change a fact? Correct it.

*Your result:* your prompt, the answer, and your correction.
:::

## 15.3 Word (lectures 7–10)

::: {.callout-important title="Main points 15.3 — Word"}
- **Formatting:** font, size, bold; paragraph alignment and line spacing.
- **Styles:** Title, Heading 1, Heading 2; change one style and all its
  headings change.
- **Lists, tables and pictures** (with Wrap Text).
- **Page layout:** margins, orientation, page breaks; **header and footer**
  with page numbers; a **table of contents** from the headings.
- A **formal letter** and a **CV** have fixed parts.
:::

![Heading styles (lecture 7).](../week-04/images/styles.png){width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.3 — Huda's report"}
1. Huda gives her ten headings the styles Heading 1 and Heading 2.
2. She inserts a table of contents (References › Table of Contents).
3. She adds a heading later and clicks **Update Table**: the contents are
   right again.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Making headings with bold and a big font. They look like headings, but Word
cannot use them for the contents or the Navigation Pane.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · A short report"}
1. Write a one-page report with a title and three headings (Heading 1).
2. Add a table of contents and page numbers in the footer.

*Your result:* `report.docx` with contents and page numbers.
:::

## 15.4 Excel (lectures 11–14)

::: {.callout-important title="Main points 15.4 — Excel"}
- A **formula** starts with = and uses cell addresses: `=B2*C2`.
- Copying changes **relative** references (B2 → B3); **absolute** ones stay
  (`$F$1`).
- **Functions:** SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN; SUMIF and COUNTIF with a rule.
- **Sort**, **filter**, **conditional formatting**; **charts**: column to
  compare, line for time, pie for parts.
:::

![Relative and absolute references (lecture 11).](../week-06/images/references.png){width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.4 — Prices with tax"}
1. The prices are in B2:B6; the tax rate (16 %) is in F1.
2. In C2: `=B2*(1+$F$1)`, copied down to C6.
3. In C7: `=SUM(C2:C6)`. If the tax changes, every cell changes by itself.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Typing a result by hand ("24") where a formula belongs. When a number
changes, the typed result stays wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Prices with tax"}
1. Type five prices and a tax rate of 16 % in F1.
2. Make the column *with tax* with one formula, copied down, and the total
   with SUM.
3. Make a column chart of the prices with a title.

*Your result:* `prices.xlsx` with formulas and a chart.
:::

## Case study: Huda's Busy Day

Huda, the office manager of the Sunrise Company, has a busy day: she names
and shares the price list, writes a notice with an AI tool and corrects a
wrong fact in it, builds a contents page for her report, copies an Excel
formula, uses a tax rate in F1, and chooses a chart for the sales of the
week. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses this day. In the
mini-game below you do each job with her.

8, 10, 12 and 14. Microsoft Support, "Office training" (support.microsoft.com).

## Exercises

1. Write a good name for a meeting note of 5 November 2026.
2. What is the difference between sync and a backup?
3. Which three parts does a clear prompt have?
4. What is a hallucination of an AI tool?
5. Why use Heading 1 and not bold text for headings?
6. Where do page numbers go?
7. What does =B2\*C2 show when B2 = 3 and C2 = 7?
8. You copy =B2\*\$F\$1 from C2 to C4. What is in C4?
9. Which function counts the cells greater than 20?
10. Which chart shows a change over time?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. `2026-11-05_meeting-note.docx`.
2. Sync copies every change (also mistakes); a backup keeps an older copy.
3. Task, context, format.
4. A made-up fact that sounds right.
5. Word uses heading styles for the contents and the Navigation Pane.
6. In the header or the footer.
7. 21.
8. =B4\*\$F\$1.
9. COUNTIF, for example =COUNTIF(E2:E11,">20").
10. A line chart.
:::
